01-001.r: Robert Bruce Foote (found the first Palaeolithic tool in India) → British geologist and archaeologist; 'father of Indian pre-history'; worked with the Geological Survey of India.

01-002.r: Three-age system (Stone, Bronze, Iron), based on the Copenhagen museum collection → coined by Christian Jurgensen Thomsen.
01-002.h: Thomsen sorted Copenhagen's museum into three ages: Stone → Bronze → Iron.

01-003.r: Alexander Rea, A.H. Longhurst, Robert Sewell, James Burgess, Walter Elliot → archaeological excavations, mainly in South Indian history.

01-004.r: Domestication of animals began in the Mesolithic period; earliest evidence → Adamgarh (Narmadapuram, M.P.) and Bagor (Bhilwara, Rajasthan).
01-004.h: A-B of domestication: Adamgarh and Bagor.

01-006.r: Mesolithic bone implements and bone ornaments → Mahadaha and Sarai Nahar Rai (Pratapgarh, U.P.); bone objects also from Damdama.

01-008.r: Mesolithic sites, west to east → Mahadaha (Pratapgarh, UP) → Lekhahia (Mirzapur, UP) → Paisra (Bihar) → Birbhanpur (W. Bengal).
01-008.h: Follow the Ganga eastward: UP, UP, Bihar, Bengal.

01-009.r: Triple burial (three skeletons in one grave) → Damdama (Pratapgarh, U.P., Mesolithic); 41 graves there, 5 double burials.
01-009.t: Don't confuse Damdama (three skeletons in one grave) with Sarai Nahar Rai (grave with four skeletons).

01-010.r: Cultivation of cereals first began in the Neolithic Age (start of agriculture); early evidence of rice and wheat → Koldihwa and Mehrgarh.

01-011.r: Earliest evidence of man (first human fossil) in India → Narmada Valley, Madhya Pradesh; discovered in 1982.

01-013.r: First cereal cultivated by man → barley (about 8000 B.C., western Asia).

01-014.r: Earliest agriculture in Indian subcontinent → Lahuradeva (Sant Kabir Nagar, U.P.; rice, 8000-7000 B.C.) per latest research; earlier answer → Mehrgarh (Balochistan, wheat).
01-014.t: If Lahuradeva is among the options, pick it; if not, pick Mehrgarh.

01-019.r: U.P. heritage: oldest agriculture evidence in global context from U.P. sites (Koldihwa in Belan valley, Lahuradev); oldest cultivated grains → barley and paddy. Both statements correct.

01-020.r: Earliest evidence of settled life → Mehrgarh (Kachhi plain, Balochistan), about 7000 B.C.; Kile Gul Muhammad 4000 B.C.; Kalibangan 3500 B.C.

01-021.r: Mesolithic domestication of animals → Bagor (Bhilwara, Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (Narmadapuram, M.P.).

01-022.r: Chalcolithic Age = Copper Age: copper tools used along with stone tools.

01-023.r: Ahar culture (Chalcolithic, Mewar, Rajasthan): knew copper smelting; metal work part of economy; black-red pottery with white geometric designs. False: rice was unknown (they knew rice).

01-024.r: Ahar-Banas culture (2100-1500 BC; Mewar, along Banas river) → contemporary of the Harappan Civilisation; sites: Ahar, Gilund, Balathal.

01-025.r: Mehrgarh (Balochistan, Pakistan) → continuous cultural remains from the Stone Age to the Harappan Civilization.

01-026.r: Navdatoli (near Khargone, Madhya Pradesh; round and rectangular huts on wooden posts) → excavated by H.D. Sankalia.

01-028.r: Megaliths → burial sites built of large stones, away from habitation; types: chamber tombs, dolmens, stone circles (cromlech), pit-circles.

01-029.r: Ash mounds (Neolithic) → Sangana Kallu (Ballari, Karnataka); also Piklihal and Utnur; burnt remains of seasonal camps of herdsmen.

01-030.r: Bhimbetka (Abdullahganj-Raisen, M.P.) → prehistoric rock paintings (elephant, sambhar, deer); most paintings of any Indian rock shelter; UNESCO World Heritage Site.

01-034.r: Bhimbetka rock shelters and their prehistoric paintings → discovered by Dr. Vishnu Shridhar Wakankar in 1957.

01-037.r: Ochre-Coloured Pottery (OCP) → named (christened) by B.B. Lal at Hastinapur, 1950-52; leaves ochre colour on fingers when rubbed.

01-038.r: Chalcolithic Maharashtra (Jorwe culture) → dead buried under house floors in north-south position (head to north); children in two urns joined mouth-to-mouth.

01-039.r: Burzahom (Kashmir, Neolithic) → dog buried with human skeleton; pit dwellings; trepanning (bored hole) marks on skeletons.

01-042.r: Palaeolithic → Sohan/Soan valley; Mesolithic → Bhimbetka caves; Neolithic → Burzahom; Chalcolithic → Banas valley.

01-043.r: Nevasa → Maharashtra; Isampur → Karnataka; Didwana → Rajasthan; Gudiyam cave → Tamil Nadu.

01-044.r: Correct: Chandraketugarh (West Bengal) → terracotta art; Ganeshwar → copper artefacts. Wrong: Burzahom is known for pit dwellings and Neolithic tools, not rock-cut shrines.

01-045.r: Correct rows: Inamgaon (Pune, Maharashtra) → Chalcolithic site; Mangadu (Kerala) → Megalithic site. Wrong: Chandraketugarh is in West Bengal, not Odisha; Salihundam row also wrong.

01-046.r: Vindhyan rock shelter with most human skeletons → Lekhahia (17 skeletons from rock shelter 1, per J.N. Pandey's 'Puratattva Vimarsh').

01-047.r: Terminal Pleistocene: Vindhyan Stone Age people migrated to the Ganga Valley because climate change made the Vindhyas dry (A and R true; R explains A).

01-048.r: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) → under Ministry of Culture; separate department in 1871 (first DG Alexander Cunningham); centralised in 1901 under Curzon.
hi: Archaeological Survey of India (भारतीय पुरातत्व सर्वेक्षण)

01-049.r: 'Father of Indian Archaeology' → Alexander Cunningham (1814-1893), British army officer with the Bengal Engineers.

01-050.r: National Museum of Mankind (Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya) → Bhopal (M.P.); autonomous body under the Ministry of Culture.

02-001.r: Book's answer: human society depends mainly on the economy; as the economy changes, society changes.

02-002.r: Harappa → Indus Valley Civilization (first evidence found at Harappa, hence 'Harappan Civilization'); one of three ancient civilizations with Egypt and Mesopotamia.

02-003.r: Indus Civilization → Proto-historic age: writing was known but is still not deciphered.

02-004.r: Indus Valley Civilization was non-Aryan because it was urban; the Aryan (Vedic) civilization was rural.

02-005.r: Book: pottery is the key reason to place the Indus civilization before the Aryans (pottery evidence from early Mehrgarh settlements onward).

02-006.r: Indus vs Vedic: Indus was urban (Vedic rural), had a pictographic script, and did not know iron (Vedic people used iron weapons) → all of the above.

02-007.r: Main source of knowledge about Harappan culture → archaeological excavations (the script is still undeciphered).

02-009.r: Main source of knowledge about Indus people → seals (over 3000 found); excavation began in 1921.

02-010.r: Origin of Harappa – wrong pair: M. Rafique Mughal → Mesopotamian inspiration. Correct: Mackay → migration from Sumer; Wheeler, Gordon → idea from West Asia; A. Ghosh → pre-Harappan matured.

02-011.r: Harappa → Daya Ram Sahni (1923-24, 1924-25); Hastinapur → B.B. Lal (1950-52); Takshashila → John Marshall (1913-34); Kaushambi → N.G. Majumdar (1936-37).

02-012.r: Earliest evidence of silver in India → Harappan culture (Mohenjodaro and Harappa).

02-013.r: Harappan pottery → mainly red (bright or dark red), wheel-made; painted pottery in red and black; polychrome rare.

02-014.r: Idol worship began in the pre-Aryan period (Indus Civilization): Mother Goddess and male and female deities worshipped.

02-015.r: Animal not shown on Harappan seals and terracotta → cow. Shown: elephant, rhinoceros, tiger, deer, sheep.

02-016.r: Sohgaura (Gorakhpur, U.P., on Rapti) → Mauryan copper-plate inscription about storehouses; not Harappan. Harappan: Chanhudaro, Kot Diji (Sindh), Desalpur (Kachchh, Gujarat).

02-017.r: Lothal → dockyard; Kalibangan → ploughed field; Dholavira → inscription of ten large Harappan signs; Banawali → terracotta plough.
02-017.h: Dholavira had the 'signboard' – ten big signs.

02-020.r: Harappa → Cemetery R-37; Lothal → dockyard; Kalibangan → furrowed land; Mohenjo-Daro → Dancing Girl statue.

02-021.r: Harappa → Ravi; Hastinapur → Ganga; Nagarjunakonda → Krishna; Paithan → Godavari.

02-022.r: Harappa → Ravi; Kalibangan → Ghaggar; Lothal → Bhogava; Ropar → Sutlej.
